posts.title: Alien Trees
posts.summary: An audio-reactive fractal tree with layered textures, glowing fruit and falling rain.
paragraphs: Another audio visualizer build. This one is a bit more trippy, and far less complex than Quantum String. It contains a central tree based on recursive fractal branching that responds to the audio, and some textured background with colour and texture variation based on incoming audio, as well as fruits.

Bass affects the branching angle, mids and transients affect branching depth, and highs affect branch-length scaling and sway. The background layers respond separately to overall RMS level, low-frequency energy and high-frequency transients, with the fruit layer driven by the high-frequency detector.

posts.title: Quantum String
posts.summary: An audio-reactive string drawn by two oscillators, with tuning shifts, wave shaping and folding.
paragraphs: After building several MIDI visualizers, I thought that probably a lot of DJs don’t use MIDI whatsoever. So to give something useful in that regard, I thought I should build audio-responsive visualizers as well. Quantum String was the first project for audio visualizers, and is still my favourite.

It’s a fairly simple concept. Two equal-amplitude sine-wave oscillators at X and Y, running at the same frequency in quadrature (90 degrees out of phase), produce a circle. Next was to make that circle react to audio in interesting ways. To do this, I let the X oscillator change frequency and phase while the Y oscillator keeps a stable base frequency. Audio-dependent waveform shaping and wave folding are then applied to both axes.

The string includes a frequency multiplier, microtuning offset, phase movement, wave folding and frequency-dependent input control for several of these parameters. Brightness follows input RMS level, and trail persistence changes with the base oscillator frequency. Low-frequency energy pulls the waveform towards a triangle, high-frequency energy towards a sawtooth, and overall level towards a square wave.

It started off looking like pure chaos, but after a ton of fine-tuning, it finally responds to music in a way that seems to reflect what you hear. I think it looks awesome, especially for downtempo or mid-tempo drum and bass music.

If you do a DJ gig, pull a screen or projector screen behind you, and have instant visuals to the music you control. Although, it is currently limited to mic input or audio from another browser tab. I’ll figure out a more universal solution soon.

posts.title: City
posts.summary: An overhead city where 88 buildings rise and light up in response to MIDI notes.
paragraphs: As I was in the zone of making MIDI-reactive visualizers, I yet again wanted to build a new concept. I was talking about a game and city structures with a friend, and thought, hey, let’s make that a MIDI visualizer as well, haha. So here it is.

It took me longer than it should have to understand how buildings look from above when they get taller and closer to you, but I got there in the end, and the formula was much simpler than what I started with.
Anyway, each building is a note on a full-size, 88-key piano. Building height depends on velocity. Hook it up to a synth or drum machine and let the city vibe with your music.

posts.title: Cube
posts.summary: A MIDI-controlled puzzle cube with rotating layers, expanding blocks and colour effects.
paragraphs: My friend was really into Rubik’s Cubes. As a nice surprise, I thought I could try to make one myself and present it to him. It was harder to build than expected, but in the end, it operates as it should, controlled by MIDI. Could be cool as it reacts to synths or other MIDI controller input.

In addition to basic face rotations, it also has middle-layer and double-row rotations, a pulse-to-solve effect, block expansion with cube rotation and block packing when rotated in expanded mode, colour inversion, and some other cool effects depending on the MIDI notes.

posts.title: Plasma Sphere
posts.summary: A MIDI-driven plasma ball with beams that drift as you hold the notes.
paragraphs: Building on the concept of 3D Plane, I thought a plasma ball would look cool reacting to incoming MIDI. Plasma beam spread, thickness and movement respond to velocity. Beam directions are set by pitch class and stay close to their starting direction at the onset of a note, but drift more as you hold notes down.

This way you can build a repetitive plasma pattern with MIDI signals, using the beams that you prefer for each note. Free to use, no setup inside the visualizer. Runs in a MIDI-capable browser and receives connected MIDI inputs once access is allowed.

posts.title: 3D Plane
posts.summary: A MIDI visualizer that folds and rotates a wireframe plane as you play.
paragraphs: As I was on a quest to find cool-looking visualizers that responded to my own music while working in the studio, it was hard to find any that were free or satisfying. As I like to build my own things, I thought, I’d rather build it myself. Before I even started, I thought, why not just let the visualizers react to the keys that I play, or MIDI notes from any controller or sequencer for that matter?

3D Plane was my first MIDI visualizer project. It folds the plane in interesting ways depending on which notes you play, and the amplitude responds to velocity. Multiple notes add their fold structures together and start rotating the plane in space.

Connect it to a drum machine or a synth, either free play or an arpeggiated sequence, and it will react directly to the incoming MIDI and sit really tight to the audio transients. If you have a gig, pull up a projector or something, and you can have stimulating visuals react to exactly what you are doing with the synths.
No installers needed, free to use. Just pull up a MIDI-capable browser, allow MIDI access if prompted, and it should receive your connected MIDI inputs right away. No setup inside the visualizer.

posts.title: Piece of Peace
posts.summary: Electric piano, recorded vocals and textures from Albion Solstice and Digitakt II.
paragraphs: Of course, I NEEDED to buy another tool. This time, Pianoteq 9 by Modartt. I tried out one of the electric pianos, and it sounded fantastic, along with the other instruments. Of course I did not need it, but I could not help myself. I recorded some vocal sounds, textures from Albion Solstice, and created textures with a Digitakt II. Further, mixing and mastering is also done by Ull Hexa, as always. Hope you like it.

posts.title: Protolanguage
posts.summary: A track inspired by AWARÉ’s hypnotic live performances.
paragraphs: I came across a performance by AWARÉ on YouTube, hours long with a hypnotic trance spread across the audience. I was inspired by the few instruments they used and how they adapted the music over time. I wanted to implement some of this into my own style of writing, testing out the new sE2200 mic by sE Electronics while I was at it.
